subtype: Crush × Caste, religion or family barrier [Actor]
passage: Usha and Pankaj had been together for a year at college in Nagpur, and her parents knew nothing. They had made it clear, more than once, that she would marry 'within our own community', and Pankaj's family wasn't. Then Amma phoned on Sunday: a family friend's son was coming to see her in three weeks. Usha felt the floor tilt. Her first instinct was to keep hiding and hope something would work itself out, or to do something dramatic in a rush. She'd seen a cousin run off, and the family still didn't speak. That evening she and Pankaj sat on the university steps with the monsoon dripping off the roof. 'Do we actually want a life together?' she asked. 'Not just now. Really.' They talked for hours: his mother, her father's temper, jobs, cities, what each of them would give up. By midnight they had a plan: Usha would tell her mother first, in person, before the visit, with her aunt beside her.

qa.q: Who was coming to see Usha in three weeks?
qa.a: A family friend's son.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Amma phoned?
qa.a: She felt shaken and anxious, as if the floor had tilted beneath her.

qa.q: What was wise about Usha and Pankaj's talk on the steps?
qa.a: They asked whether they truly wanted a life together and planned how to tell her family, instead of hiding or running off.

qa.q: How might Usha's mother feel when Usha tells her in person?
qa.a: Probably shocked and worried about the community, but told honestly rather than facing a sudden crisis.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose family may not accept her partner's community, choosing serious talk and a plan over secrecy or a sudden crisis.

subtype: Crush × Caste, religion or family barrier [Actor]
passage: On the rooftop of the office block where they were both interning in Chennai, Raghav said it again: 'Let's not tell anyone till we both have jobs. Maybe three, four years. Then they'll have to accept us.' Lavanya watched the traffic on Anna Salai below. They had been together eight months. Her family went to church every Sunday; his mother did a long puja every morning and had said at a wedding once that 'mixed marriages never last'. Lavanya loved him. But she also knew what years of lying could do: her cousin had tried it, and when it came out the whole family exploded at once. 'Raghav, I don't want a secret that blows up. Can we talk about what we actually want? Religion for kids, festivals, where we'd live, who we tell first?' He was quiet a long time. Then he pulled out his phone and opened a blank note. 'Okay. A list. Let's be serious.' They stayed on the roof till the sky turned orange.

qa.q: What did Raghav's mother once say at a wedding?
qa.a: That 'mixed marriages never last'.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya feel uneasy about Raghav's plan?
qa.a: She loved him but feared a long secret would explode, as it had in her cousin's family.

qa.q: What did Lavanya propose instead of years of secrecy?
qa.a: Talking seriously about what they want: religion for kids, festivals, where to live and who to tell first.

qa.q: How does Raghav respond to Lavanya's request?
qa.a: After a long silence he agrees, opening a note to make a serious list together.

grounding: Shows a young woman in an interfaith relationship who rejects long secrecy and asks her partner to think seriously about family and a shared future.

passage: First week of term. Tarun posted a photo of Vasudha with 'Mine forever' and a crown sticker. She laughed, but looked uneasy. When she said she'd joined a theatre group that rehearsed late, he sulked: 'You'll have no time for me.' Three weeks later. Vasudha's grandmother fell ill, and she had to go home to Mysore mid-semester. Tarun took her lab notes every day, typed them up, and called each night at nine as promised, even when she only wanted to cry. He stopped posting about them. It didn't feel like the point any more. Two months later. Vasudha was back, and on opening night he sat in the front row of her play with his roommate, clapping until his hands hurt. Afterwards he told her, 'I was scared the theatre thing meant losing you. It didn't. It's more you.' She squeezed his hand. 'You showed up every single day. That's what I'll remember.'

qa.q: What did Tarun post in the first week of term?
qa.a: A photo of Vasudha with 'Mine forever' and a crown sticker.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Vasudha joined the theatre group?
qa.a: He felt insecure and afraid of losing her, which came out as sulking.

qa.q: How did Tarun's idea of love change over the weeks?
qa.a: From posting and possessiveness to reliability: daily notes, nightly calls and supporting her theatre.

qa.q: What will Vasudha remember most?
qa.a: That he showed up every single day when things were hard.

grounding: Shows a young man whose love shifts from possessive posts to reliability, honest talk and making room for his partner's growth.

passage: Raghav, you asked what love is, as if I keep a definition in the almirah. Listen instead. I married your Dadu at twenty, in Guwahati. Everyone thinks love is the wedding, the songs. For us it was the second year, when I wanted to finish my teaching degree and his mother said a daughter-in-law belongs in the kitchen. Your Dadu could have stayed quiet. Instead he sat with her and said, 'Binita will study. I'll cook on her exam days.' And he did, terrible dal and all, for two years. He never once showed me off to the neighbours. But he walked me to the exam hall every morning at seven. That's what I learned, Raghav. Love is who keeps showing up, and who makes room for you to grow. Not who shouts it loudest. Now go, phone your girl, and ask how her exam went.

qa.q: What did Dadu promise to do on Binita's exam days?
qa.a: Cook, even if the dal was terrible.

qa.q: What does Binita feel looking back on those two years?
qa.a: Binita feels grateful and deeply loved, remembering how Dadu kept showing up.

qa.q: What choice in Binita's story showed real commitment?
qa.a: Dadu backing Binita's teaching degree against his mother, then walking her to every exam.

qa.q: How did Dadu's mother seem to see Binita at first?
qa.a: As a daughter-in-law who belonged in the kitchen, not someone who should study.

grounding: An elder's story showing love as reliable support and room to grow, not as display or ownership.

passage: Student counselling note, Monday. Suraj (third year, commerce) came in to talk about his relationship with Tanvir, now six months long. He described Tanvir planning surprise dinners, remembering every exam date, and recently saying he sees a future with him. Suraj said it feels warm and also frightening: he has never felt that chosen before and worries he can't match it. He admitted he had skipped two football evenings with his friends to be available, and felt quietly resentful. We talked about receiving care honestly: thanking Tanvir, saying clearly what he can and can't give right now, and keeping his own friendships rather than disappearing into the relationship. Suraj decided to tell Tanvir this week, 'I love how you show up for me. I'm slower with big words, and I need my Thursday football.' He left looking lighter. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: What has Suraj skipped to be available for Tanvir?
qa.a: Two football evenings with his friends.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel about being so chosen by Tanvir?
qa.a: He feels warm and also frightened, worried he can't match Tanvir's devotion.

qa.q: What did Suraj plan to tell Tanvir, and why is it healthy?
qa.a: That he loves how Tanvir shows up but is slower with big words and needs his Thursday football, being honest about limits and keeping friendships.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel hearing Suraj's words?
qa.a: Possibly a little unsure at first, but reassured by the honesty and the thanks.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a young man who feels chosen by his partner, receiving it with honesty about his limits and keeping his friendships.

passage:
Tuesday night. Rashmi surprised me today with a whole notebook of things she'd noticed about me over the year: the way I hum when I'm nervous, how I always give the last samosa away. I cried in the library. Nobody has ever paid that much attention to me. And then, on the walk back, a small scary feeling: what if I can't give her this much back? What if she expects me every evening now? I noticed I'd already said no to Meera's birthday dinner on Friday because Rashmi had 'maybe' plans. That's not fair to Meera, or to me. So tonight I called Rashmi and said it honestly: 'I love this. I love you. I'm also someone who needs my friends and quiet evenings, and I'm not great at grand gestures.' She laughed and said she knew, and that's partly why she likes me. I'm going to Meera's dinner. I wrote Rashmi a small thank-you note back.
- Aadhya

qa.q: What did Rashmi give Aadhya?
qa.a: A notebook of things she'd noticed over the year.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel on the walk back from the library?
qa.a: Aadhya felt warm and loved, but also a small fear of not being able to give as much back.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do to receive the love honestly?
qa.a: Told Rashmi about needing friends and quiet evenings, kept Meera's dinner plan, and wrote a small thank-you note.

qa.q: How does Rashmi react to Aadhya's honesty?
qa.a: She laughs and says she already knew, and that it's part of why she likes Aadhya 🙂

grounding: A diary of a young person who feels deeply chosen, receiving it with honesty about their limits and keeping their own friendships.

passage: Honestly? Trust didn't come naturally to me. I'm Eshaan, and in first year I was the person who checked my partner's last-seen every ten minutes. Kiran would go to a study group and I'd send, 'who's there? send a pic?' Once I even made up a fake emergency to see how fast Kiran would call back. That's not love, that's a test. Kiran finally said, 'I can't pass an exam every day.' That scared me into thinking. So I started noticing the small stuff instead: Kiran always called when promised, always turned up at nine for our Sunday walk, and told me the awkward things too, like forgetting to book my birthday dinner. Trust grew out of those. It isn't blind, though. If Kiran started lying about big things, I'd notice, and I'd say so. But I don't need proof every hour any more. That feels so much lighter.

qa.q: What did Eshaan once make up to test Kiran?
qa.a: A fake emergency, to see how fast Kiran would call back.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling underneath the constant checking in first year?
qa.a: Eshaan felt insecure and anxious, needing proof every hour to feel safe.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan build real trust?
qa.a: Noticing Kiran's small kept promises, like calls and Sunday walks, while staying alert to real red flags.

qa.q: How did Kiran experience Eshaan's tests?
qa.a: As exhausting, like having to pass an exam every day.

grounding: A spoken account of a young person who stops testing a partner and builds trust through small kept promises, without becoming blind to red flags.

passage: October. Nazia started staying late at the physics lab three nights a week, and Farhan felt a knot every time. Who else was there? He almost asked to see her phone. Instead he said, 'I trust you,' and decided to find out whether he meant it. November. He paid attention. She texted at ten every lab night, as promised. She told him when her lab partner's jokes made her uncomfortable, and what she'd said back. She came to his cousin's wedding straight from an experiment, still in her lab coat. The knot loosened. December. One night she forgot to text, and his old panic flared. He wanted to fire off ten messages. He sent one: 'All okay?' Her reply came an hour later: 'Sorry! Phone died. I'm fine, walking to the hostel with Divya.' He noticed he'd been ready to believe the worst. He also noticed he didn't need to. Her record spoke for her.

qa.q: What did Nazia do every lab night?
qa.a: She texted Farhan at ten, as promised.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when Nazia forgot to text in December?
qa.a: His old panic flared and he felt anxious, ready to believe the worst.

qa.q: How did Farhan handle the missed text better than before?
qa.a: He sent one calm 'All okay?' instead of ten messages, trusting her record of kept promises.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Farhan's single message?
qa.a: As caring rather than controlling, making it easy to reply honestly.

grounding: Shows a young man building trust in his partner through small kept promises over weeks, and responding calmly instead of testing her.

passage:
Dear Jatin,
I've been thinking since our fight on Sunday, and I want to say something I couldn't say out loud.
I've made you my everything, and that isn't fair to you. When you're busy, my whole day goes grey. I haven't decided a single thing this semester without asking you first, not even which elective to take. I stopped going to my Wednesday dance class because it clashed with your free evening. When you said you wanted a weekend with your school friends, I sulked as if you were leaving me.
That's not you doing anything wrong. That's me handing you my whole happiness and then being angry when you can't hold it.
So I'm changing things. I've rejoined dance. I'm going home to Indore for my sister's birthday on my own. I chose the elective myself, the one I actually like.
I want to love you because I choose you, not because I can't stand up without you.
Jyoti

qa.q: Which class did Jyoti stop going to?
qa.a: The Wednesday dance class, because it clashed with Jatin's free evening.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when Jatin wanted a weekend with school friends?
qa.a: Jyoti felt abandoned and sulked, as if being left.

qa.q: What changes is Jyoti making, and why do they help?
qa.a: Rejoining dance, visiting home alone and choosing the elective, so life has its own anchors beyond Jatin.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Likely relieved and touched, freed from carrying Jyoti's whole happiness.

grounding: A letter from a young person who has leaned on a partner for mood and decisions, choosing to rebuild their own friends and goals.

passage: So, Meghna, you want to know why I'm at the gym at seven? It's a long story, but I'm Kalyani and you're my oldest friend, so sit. When Pankaj left for his internship in Hyderabad in May, I fell apart. Not heartbreak; nothing happened between us. I just realised I didn't know what to do with myself. For a year he'd chosen our films, our food, even whether I should cut my hair. When he didn't reply for four hours, my whole mood dropped. On day three I cried because I couldn't decide what to have for dinner. That's when I thought: this isn't love, this is leaning so hard I've forgotten how to stand. So I started small. Joined the gym. Called you. Picked up the sketching I'd dropped in second year. When Pankaj came back, I told him all of it. He said, 'You seem more you.' I think that's the best thing he's ever said.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj go for his internship?
qa.a: To Hyderabad, in May.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel on day three of Pankaj's internship?
qa.a: Kalyani felt lost and helpless, crying over not being able to decide what to have for dinner.

qa.q: What small steps helped Kalyani stop depending so heavily on Pankaj?
qa.a: Joining the gym, calling Meghna, and picking up sketching again.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Kalyani when he returns?
qa.a: He says Kalyani seems 'more you', noticing a fuller, more independent self.

grounding: A spoken account of a young person who realises they depend on a partner for mood and decisions and rebuilds their own interests and friendships.

passage:
'You're going to the hackathon? For the whole weekend?' Tejas's voice cracked over the phone.
'It's the one I told you about in June,' Sumit said gently.
'But what am I supposed to do? You know Sundays are hard for me.'
Sumit closed his eyes. For months he'd cancelled things: football, his cousin's engagement, sleep. 'Tej, I care about you so much. I want to help. But I can't be the only thing holding your weekend together. I'm getting really tired.'
Silence. Then, small: 'So I'm too much.'
'No. You're not too much. It's just too much for one person. Who else could you call on Sunday? Your sister? The guys from the band?'
'...Rohit asked me to jam, actually.'
'Say yes. And that counselling cell you mentioned? Maybe book a slot this week.'
'You'll still call Saturday night?'
'Nine o'clock. I promise. And I'll tell you everything about the hackathon.'

qa.q: What event is Sumit going to for the whole weekend?
qa.a: A hackathon he'd mentioned in June.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling before he spoke up?
qa.a: He felt tired and weighed down after months of cancelling his own plans.

qa.q: How did Sumit set a limit kindly?
qa.a: He said he cared but couldn't be the only support, suggested Tejas's sister, band friends and the counselling cell, and promised a Saturday call.

qa.q: How does Tejas first hear Sumit's limit?
qa.a: As 'I'm too much', a painful fear of being a burden.

grounding: Shows a young man whose partner needs him constantly, giving care while naming his limit kindly and encouraging other supports.

passage: In my final year, I nearly gave up my place on the university football team out of guilt. I'm Thomas, and my girlfriend Seema was going through a hard year: her father had lost his job, and she wanted me with her every free minute. If I went to training, she'd text, 'I guess football matters more.' So I stopped going. Then I stopped seeing my friends. I told myself that's what love looks like. By March I was exhausted and snapping at her, which helped no one. My sister sat me down and said, 'You're allowed to care and still have a life. Actually, you have to, or you'll have nothing left to give.' So I talked to Seema, carefully. I said I'd be there for her every evening at eight, but I was going back to training. I also helped her find the student counselling service. She was hurt at first. A few weeks later she thanked me; she'd made two friends in a counselling group. We were both breathing again.

qa.q: What did Seema text when Thomas went to training?
qa.a: 'I guess football matters more.'

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling by March?
qa.a: Thomas felt exhausted and guilty, snapping at Seema after giving up football and friends.

qa.q: How did Thomas balance care with a limit?
qa.a: Promised to be there every evening at eight, returned to training, and helped Seema find the counselling service.

qa.q: How did Seema come to see the change?
qa.a: She was hurt at first, but later thanked Thomas after making friends in a counselling group.

grounding: A first-person account of a partner's heavy need, where guilt nearly costs the narrator their own life, and a kind limit plus other supports helps both.

passage: Sharmila had forty-eight hours to accept the job in Bengaluru, and her first instinct was to assume Rehana would simply come along. They'd been together three years; Rehana could find work anywhere, right? Then, packing boxes in their shared room in Pune, Sharmila saw the letter on Rehana's desk: a fellowship offer from a Delhi research lab, deadline the same week. Rehana hadn't even mentioned it. 'Why didn't you tell me?' 'I thought you'd already decided for both of us,' Rehana said quietly. That stung, because it was true. That evening they sat on the floor with two sheets of paper: Sharmila's plans, Rehana's plans, and what each would cost. For the first time Sharmila really listened to Rehana talk about the lab: the project on monsoon patterns, the professor she admired. By midnight they had agreed: Delhi for two years, while Sharmila asked her firm about its Gurgaon office. The next move would be Sharmila's call.

qa.q: What offer had Rehana received?
qa.a: A fellowship from a Delhi research lab, with a deadline the same week.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Rehana said she thought it was already decided?
qa.a: It stung, because Sharmila knew it was true.

qa.q: What made the final decision fair?
qa.a: They listed both plans and costs, Sharmila truly listened to Rehana's ambitions, and they agreed to take turns choosing the move.

qa.q: Why hadn't Rehana mentioned the fellowship?
qa.a: She felt her ambitions didn't count because Sharmila had already decided for both of them.

grounding: Shows a young woman who assumed her partner would follow her career, then listens to her partner's ambitions and shares the decision fairly.

passage: In their small rented flat near Majnu ka Tilla in Delhi, Aadhya noticed a pattern one Sunday: Dolma had cooked every dinner that week, paid the electricity bill, and still stayed up finishing her nursing assignments. Aadhya had spent her evenings on her design portfolio. She'd told herself it balanced out. It didn't. At dinner she put down her spoon. 'Can we look at who does what? I think I've been leaving you most of it.' Dolma laughed, surprised, then admitted she'd been too tired to raise it. They made a list on the back of a takeaway menu: cooking, bills, laundry, the landlord. They split it by week, not by who cared more. Then Aadhya asked about Dolma's plan to apply for intensive care training. 'You'd have night shifts?' 'Yes.' 'Then I'll handle the mornings, the milk and the water cans.' Dolma looked at her. 'You're serious?' 'Your career counts as much as mine.'

qa.q: What did they write their chore list on?
qa.a: The back of a takeaway menu.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she noticed the pattern?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and a bit guilty, seeing she had been leaving Dolma most of the work.

qa.q: How did Aadhya make the partnership more equal?
qa.a: She raised it, split chores by week, and offered to cover mornings so Dolma could pursue intensive care training.

qa.q: How does Dolma react when Aadhya offers to take the mornings?
qa.a: She's surprised and touched, checking whether Aadhya is serious 😊

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing an unfair split with her partner, sharing effort fairly and backing her partner's career ambitions.

passage: Can I tell you what I finally understood this year? I'm Sabina, and for most of my relationship with Sangeeta I kept a secret scoreboard. I cooked twice, she cooked once. I remembered her mum's birthday, she forgot my exam date. I'd sulk and not even say why. Then in April my grandmother died, and I had to fly to Kochi with two days' notice. Sangeeta rearranged her whole week. She packed my bag while I sat on the floor, and she emailed my professors. She sent me a voice note every night, not asking for anything, just humming the song I like. When I came back, there was food in the fridge labelled with the days. I sat down and wrote her a list, a real one: 'Thank you for the bag. For the emails. For the humming.' Then I threw away the scoreboard. Last month, during her exams, I did the fridge for her.

qa.q: What had Sangeeta labelled in the fridge?
qa.a: Food, labelled with the days.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel coming back to the labelled food?
qa.a: Sabina felt deeply grateful and moved, finally seeing everything Sangeeta had quietly done.

qa.q: How did Sabina replace the scoreboard?
qa.a: By thanking Sangeeta specifically in a written list and returning the care during her exams.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt about the old silent sulking?
qa.a: Probably confused and hurt, since Sabina never said why.

grounding: A spoken account of a young person who drops a scoreboard of favours after noticing a partner's quiet support, thanking her specifically and reciprocating.

passage: Early September. Yash kept a mental ledger. He'd driven Sangeeta to the airport twice; she'd driven him once. When she forgot to bring his favourite pastries back from her trip, he went quiet for a whole evening. Mid-September. Yash's father was admitted to hospital in Nashik, and Yash had exams the same week. Sangeeta didn't ask what she could do. She just did it: sat with him in the hospital canteen at midnight, quizzed him on accounting formulas from his notes, and texted his mother every morning to ask if they'd eaten. She never mentioned any of it afterwards. October. Yash's father was home and recovering. Yash sat Sangeeta down at their usual chai stall and said, 'Thank you. For the canteen at midnight, for the formulas, for texting my mother. I noticed all of it.' She shrugged, embarrassed. The next week, when her thesis deadline hit, Yash quietly took over the grocery runs and never counted them.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do for Yash's mother every morning?
qa.a: Texted her to ask if they'd eaten.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Sangeeta forgot the pastries?
qa.a: He felt resentful and short-changed, keeping score of favours.

qa.q: How did Yash show gratitude well in October?
qa.a: He named each thing Sangeeta had done, then quietly took over the grocery runs during her deadline.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta react to Yash's thanks?
qa.a: She shrugs, embarrassed, since she never expected anything back.

grounding: Shows a young man moving from keeping score to thanking his partner specifically for quiet support and reciprocating.

passage: Salma had read Arman's messages over his shoulder twice that week, and last night she'd picked a fight about a colleague's 'good morning' text, just to see if he'd still say he loved her. He did. It didn't help. On Sunday, over coffee at a Bandra café, her friend Nikita asked why she looked so tired. Salma found herself saying it: 'I keep thinking he'll leave. So I either cling or I push, to test him.' Nikita didn't laugh. 'What would you tell me if I said that?' 'That he's not the problem. The fear is.' Salma went quiet. That evening, instead of checking his phone, she told Arman the truth: 'I'm scared you'll leave, and I've been acting badly because of it. It's not about you. I'm working on it.' Arman held her hand. 'Thank you for saying it. I'm not going anywhere. But I'd like you to talk to someone too, not just me.' She booked a counselling session the next day.

qa.q: What did Salma pick a fight about?
qa.a: A colleague's 'good morning' text to Arman.

qa.q: What was Salma afraid of underneath the clinging and testing?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid that Arman would leave.

qa.q: What did Salma do instead of checking his phone?
qa.a: She named her fear honestly to Arman, took responsibility, and booked a counselling session.

qa.q: How does Arman respond to Salma's honesty?
qa.a: He thanks her, reassures her, and gently suggests she talk to someone besides him.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose fear of losing her partner leads to phone-checking and fights, until she names the fear, talks openly and seeks help.

passage:
'You're always on your phone lately,' Kamal snapped, tossing the dish towel on the counter.
Mohit looked up. 'I'm replying to the London office about joining dates. You know that.'
'Right. London. Where you'll forget me in a month.'
'Kamal. Where's this coming from?'
Kamal opened his mouth for another jab, then stopped. He sat down at the small kitchen table. 'Honestly? I'm scared. Ever since you got the offer, I keep waiting for you to leave me. So I pick fights. It's like I'm trying to make it happen first so it hurts less.'
Mohit pulled out the other chair. 'That's a lot to carry.'
'I don't want to be this person.'
'Then let's talk instead of fighting. What would help?'
'Knowing the plan. Visits. Calls. And maybe having something of my own here, so I'm not just waiting.'
'That pottery class you keep mentioning?'
'Yeah.' Kamal almost smiled. 'That.'

qa.q: What was Mohit replying to on his phone?
qa.a: The London office, about joining dates.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling underneath the snapping?
qa.a: He was scared of Mohit leaving, and picked fights to make it hurt less first.

qa.q: What helped the conversation turn around?
qa.a: Kamal named his fear instead of jabbing, and they talked about a plan, visits, calls and his own pottery class.

qa.q: How does Mohit respond to Kamal's fear?
qa.a: Calmly and warmly, calling it a lot to carry and inviting him to talk.

grounding: Shows a young man whose fear of losing his partner comes out as fights, until he names it and they talk openly about a plan.

passage: August. Gurleen moved to Toronto for her master's, and Vinita stayed in Chandigarh for her final year. The time difference was nine and a half hours. Vinita sent twenty messages a day and felt betrayed every time Gurleen took six hours to reply. One night she typed, 'Guess I'm not a priority any more,' and hit send. September. On a rare long call, Gurleen cried. 'I'm in labs all day, then working at the café. I'm not forgetting you. I'm drowning.' Vinita heard it. They made a deal: one proper video call every Sunday at 9 p.m. her time, voice notes whenever, no guilt for slow replies. November. The voice notes had become their diary: Vinita's thesis panic, Gurleen's first snowfall, the new friend she'd made in class. They had booked Gurleen's flight home for the winter break. Vinita still missed her every day. But silence no longer felt like a verdict.

qa.q: When did they agree to have a proper video call?
qa.a: Every Sunday at 9 p.m. Vinita's time.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when Gurleen took six hours to reply?
qa.a: She felt forgotten and hurt, reading the silence as betrayal.

qa.q: What deal made the distance easier?
qa.a: A realistic plan: one weekly video call, voice notes whenever, no guilt for slow replies, and a booked visit 👍

qa.q: What was Gurleen's side of the slow replies?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed by labs and work, not forgetting Vinita but drowning.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a long-distance relationship who moves from demanding replies to a realistic contact plan, shared inner lives and a planned visit.

passage: Nitin, you think long distance started with your video calls? When I was twenty-one, your Nanaji was posted in Leh with the army, and I was finishing my BA in Ludhiana. No phones. Letters took three weeks, sometimes six in winter. Once, two months passed with nothing. I was sure he'd found someone else. I wrote him a furious letter, and my mother caught me on the way to post it. She said, 'Jasleen, snow blocks roads. It doesn't block hearts.' So I tore it up and wrote instead about my exams, the neighbours' goat, my fears about the future. Every week, whether he wrote or not. When his letters finally came, eight arrived together, one for every week. We'd agreed on nothing, and still we had both kept writing. After that we promised: one letter a week each, and his leave in April. So, beta, stop counting her replies. Agree on what's realistic, tell her about your real days, and plan the next visit.
